extracted.intended_audience: general Victorian reading public; readers interested in London fairs, private theatres, and social satire
extracted.subtask_short: victorian sketches of fairs and theatre
extracted.subtask_description: Literary sketches describing Greenwich Fair, private theatres, travelling shows, and Vauxhall Gardens—observational satire that also records theatrical and showman conventions useful for producing low melodrama and popular entertainments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Melodrama formula / stock-plot elements
rubrics_metrics.description: The story of the tragedy is always pretty much the same. There is a rightful heir, who loves a young lady, and is beloved by her; and a wrongful heir, who loves her too, and isn’t beloved by her; and the wrongful heir gets hold of the rightful heir, and throws him into a dungeon ... then the rightful heir is discovered in prison, carefully holding a long chain in his hands, and seated despondingly in a large arm-chair; and the young lady comes in to two bars of soft music ... the wrongful heir comes in to two bars of quick music (technically called ‘a hurry’) ... then a tall white figure ... slowly rises ... This is no other than the ghost of the rightful heir’s father ... and then a muffin-bell rings, and the curtain drops.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this set of stock characters and beats (rightful vs wrongful heir, dungeon, chain, soft music for reunion, quick music for villain's entrance, ghost rising with blue fire, a muffled musical cue and curtain drop) to construct a recognizably effective melodrama; audience expectation is met by these recurrent elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of stage-effects and priced bits
rubrics_metrics.description: Such are the written placards ... and such are the sums extracted ... by the donkeys who are prevailed upon to pay for permission to exhibit their lamentable ignorance ... For instance, the Duke of Glo’ster is well worth two pounds, because he has it all to himself; he must wear a real sword, and what is better still, he must draw it, several times in the course of the piece. The soliloquies alone are well worth fifteen shillings; then there is the stabbing King Henry—decidedly cheap at three-and-sixpence ... The tent scene is confessedly worth half-a-sovereign, and so you have the fight in, gratis ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritise spectacular, repeatable visual and vocal set-pieces (sword-drawing, soliloquies, stagings of stabbings, tent scene) because they reliably produce audience approval and are treated as the theatre’s money-making 'bits'. Proportion staging effort to the dramatic 'value' of each effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combat choreography and prolongation for effect
rubrics_metrics.description: One—two—three—four—over; then, one—two—three—four—under; then thrust; then dodge and slide about; then fall down on one knee; then fight upon it, and then get up again and stagger. You may keep on doing this, as long as it seems to take—say ten minutes—and then fall down (backwards, if you can manage it without hurting yourself), and die game: nothing like it for producing an effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stretch and stylise stage combats with repetitive measured beats and varied movements; include an arresting final fall (backwards, gamely performed) to maximize audience reaction. Use children or a female in white to increase pathos and interest in combats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delivery and business for key lines
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Orf with his ed’ (very quick and loud;—then slow and sneeringly)—‘So much for Bu-u-u-uckingham!’ Lay the emphasis on the ’uck; get yourself gradually into a corner, and work with your right hand, while you’re saying it, as if you were feeling your way, and it’s sure to do.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Performance of famous one-liners requires precise vocal contrast (quick then drawn sneer), physical business (edging into a corner; right-hand movement) and emphasis on specific syllables to elicit applause; mimic established stage conventions rather than inventing subtler realism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ghost-effect conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: A blue smoke is seen, a gong is heard, and a tall white figure (who has been all this time, behind the arm-chair, covered over with a table-cloth), slowly rises to the tune of ‘Oft in the stilly night.’ ... the ghost (who can’t do anything without blue fire) blesses the rightful heir and the young lady, by half suffocating them with smoke.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ simple, obvious visual tricks (white-sheeted figure, blue smoke, specific musical cue) to signify supernatural presence; exaggeration and sensory cues (smoke suffocating the lovers) are effective because audiences accept and enjoy the theatrical artifice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stage-management and cueing procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Now,’ cries the manager, consulting the written list ... ‘Scene 1, open country—lamps down—thunder and lightning—all ready, White?’ ... ‘Clear the stage,’ cries the manager, hastily packing every member of the company into the little space there is between the wings and the wall, and one wing and another. ‘Places, places. Now then, Witches—Duncan—Malcolm—bleeding officer—where’s the bleeding officer?’ ... The bell rings, and the orchestra, in acknowledgment of the call, play three distinct chords. The bell rings—the tragedy (!) opens—
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain a written scene list, call scenes and props aloud, check readiness with named crew, use a ringing bell to summon orchestra responses (three chords) and to signal lift/curtain—clear, repeated verbal cues and simple musical acknowledgements coordinate a small company and noisy house.

rubrics_metrics.name: Casting by distant resemblance
rubrics_metrics.description: The large woman, who is consulting the stage directions ... is the Lady Macbeth of the night; she is always selected to play the part, because she is tall and stout, and looks a little like Mrs. Siddons—at a considerable distance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select performers whose general physical outline or presence approximates famed models when viewed from the audience; coarse resemblances and stage distance can substitute for skill when expectation and spectacle matter more than authenticity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Showmanship techniques for travelling menageries
rubrics_metrics.description: The principal officer ... is generally a very tall, hoarse man, in a scarlet coat, with a cane in his hand, with which he occasionally raps the pictures we have just noticed, by way of illustrating his description—something in this way. ‘Here, here, here; the lion, the lion (tap), exactly as he is represented on the canvas outside (three taps): no waiting, remember; no deception. The fe-ro-cious lion (tap, tap) who bit off the gentleman’s head last Cambervel vos a twelvemonth, and has killed on the awerage three keepers a-year ever since he arrived at matoority. No extra charge on this account recollect; the price of admission is only sixpence.’ This address never fails to produce a considerable sensation, and sixpences flow into the treasury with wonderful rapidity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a hoarse, authoritative announcer, theatrical tapping, sensational (often doubtful) anecdote, repetition, and a low admission price to attract and convert crowds; rhetorical bravado and visible spectacle on canvas are reliable marketing tools.

rubrics_metrics.name: Con/plant technique in street games
rubrics_metrics.description: Here some greenhorn whispers his friend that he distinctly saw the pea roll under the middle thimble—an impression which is immediately confirmed by a gentleman in top-boots ... The ‘plant’ is successful, the bet is made, the stranger of course loses: and the gentleman with the thimbles consoles him, as he pockets the money, with an assurance that it’s ‘all the fortin of war! this time I vin, next time you vin: niver mind the loss of two bob and a bender! Do it up in a small parcel, and break out in a fresh place.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To persuade onlookers to bet, stage a corroborating observer (a planted confederate with plausible status), encourage the target’s confidence, accept the wager publicly, and use a convivial consoling patter after the loss to deflect suspicion and move on to a new location.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spectacle-scaling for exhibited curiosities
rubrics_metrics.description: The best thing about a dwarf is, that he has always a little box, about two feet six inches high, into which, by long practice, he can just manage to get, by doubling himself up like a boot-jack; this box is painted outside like a six-roomed house ... As a giant is not so easily moved, a pair of indescribables of most capacious dimensions, and a huge shoe, are usually brought out, into which two or three stout men get all at once, to the enthusiastic delight of the crowd, who are quite satisfied with the solemn assurance that these habiliments form part of the giant’s everyday costume.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create convincing displays for curiosities by supplying scaled props (miniature house-boxes for dwarfs, giant shoe for large exhibits) and perform suggestive domestic actions; audiences readily accept the staged illusion when props reinforce the claimed identity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporary ballroom (fair ball) entertainment style
rubrics_metrics.description: The grandest and most numerously-frequented booth in the whole fair, however, is ‘The Crown and Anchor’—a temporary ball-room ... There is no master of the ceremonies in this artificial Eden—all is primitive, unreserved, and unstudied. The dust is blinding, the heat insupportable, the company somewhat noisy, and in the highest spirits possible: the ladies, in the height of their innocent animation, dancing in the gentlemen’s hats, and the gentlemen promenading ‘the gay and festive scene’ in the ladies’ bonnets, or with the more expensive ornaments of false noses, and low-crowned, tinder-box-looking hats ... The dancing, itself, beggars description—every figure lasts about an hour, and the ladies bounce up and down the middle, with a degree of spirit which is quite indescribable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For over-the-top communal dance entertainments, abandon strict formality: permit cross-dressing ornamentation, improvisatory figures, loud mixed music, and long repetitive dances; the chaotic, exuberant atmosphere is part of the draw and should be maintained rather than disciplined.
